comment: Defects found in this repository's own skills and installer.

bugs.title: The shipped core library lost plan_stat_mode and plan_stat_uid, so an installed skill could not read a file mode
bugs.observed: 0 definitions. Two tests said so: test-portable-helpers.sh reported plan_stat_mode: command not found for three assertions, and test-duplication-ratchet.sh reported it is referenced by MAINTAINER.md section 3 but no longer exists.
bugs.expected: Both helpers present in the compiled library; plan_atomic_write calls plan_stat_mode to preserve a file mode.
bugs.mechanism: The re-marking script kept PACKAGE: DEV on any path matching *probe* -- intended for a planted test fixture named plan_probe_dev_only.sh -- and planning/scripts/lib/core/plan_stat_probe.sh matched on its name. PACKAGE: DEV means dev-build-only, so the prod build excluded it.
bugs.fix: Marked plan_stat_probe.sh PACKAGE: PROD and rebuilt. Every other compiler input was checked for the same mistake; it was the only one.
bugs.verification: test-portable-helpers.sh and test-duplication-ratchet.sh both pass; five stat-helper definitions and calls are back in plan-core-lib.sh. Re-marking the file PACKAGE: DEV reproduces the failure.
bugs.found_by: the both-shell run of the release commit, on both bash 5.3 and 3.2
bugs.notes: A name-substring match standing in for a marker. The marker was right in every file; the script that wrote it guessed from the filename. It also shows the release checks were not sufficient on their own: build-release.sh --list and a by-hand diff of npm pack both passed a library with a function missing, because they compare file sets and not file contents.

bugs.title: BSD awk rejects a newline inside a string, so a table cell breaks plan-content on macOS
bugs.reproduce: CI run 32394476430, job "Test suite passes on macos-latest": planning/tests/test-plan-commands.sh
bugs.observed: awk: newline in string | A | B |  — then the test failed (exit 64).
bugs.expected: The row is written as it is under GNU awk.
bugs.mechanism: Not yet located. A literal newline reaches an awk string, which one-true-awk on macOS refuses and GNU awk accepts. The candidates are the awk calls that build or rewrite a table row.
bugs.found_by: the macOS leg of CI, the first execution of this code on BSD userland
bugs.notes: Cannot be reproduced on this machine: it needs BSD awk. Diagnose from the CI log or a macOS runner, not by guessing here.

bugs.title: A plans-root path comparison fails on macOS, where TMPDIR carries a trailing slash and /var is a symlink
bugs.observed: assertion failed: grep -Fqx "demo-plan|$plan_root/plan-description.md|$plan_root/steps". The log shows paths like /var/folders/.../T//ai-skills-tests.XmQi3B — note the double slash.
bugs.expected: The helper output holds the plan paths exactly as the test builds them.
bugs.mechanism: Two candidates, both macOS-specific and both plausible: TMPDIR ends with a slash there, so "$TMPDIR/x" yields a double slash; and /var is a symlink to /private/var, so pwd -P resolves a path the test built literally. An -Fx comparison is exact, so either is enough.
bugs.notes: Worth a portability rule once the mechanism is settled: every literal path comparison in the suite has the same exposure.

bugs.title: BSD grep rejects an empty subexpression, so the progress fallback pattern never matches on macOS
bugs.observed: grep: empty (sub)expression, then FAIL: rebuild-plan-progress falls back to goal name for a bare goal.
bugs.mechanism: A pattern contains an empty alternation branch, which GNU grep tolerates and BSD grep refuses outright. Same family as the bre-alternation rule added today, and equally silent: the pattern matches nothing rather than erroring where it is built.
bugs.fix: The pattern is passed to check(), which greps with -E, so its pipes are escaped: a leading bare | is an empty alternation branch. One offender in the repo; the other helpers that take a pipe-leading pattern grep with a BRE, where | is literal, and are unaffected.
bugs.verification: test-progress-derivation passes, and the escaped pattern still matches the row. The unescaped form is rejected here too by ugrep (error at position 4), so the fix is strictly more portable, not merely macOS-specific.
bugs.notes: Candidate for a gated portability rule: an empty branch is textually detectable, unlike the general BRE-alternation case.

bugs.title: No maintainer document mentions the registers, so a change that resolves or finds a bug leaves BUGS.json and TODO.json untouched
bugs.reproduce: grep -c "BUGS.json\|TODO.json\|bug-report" planning/MAINTAINER.md CONTRIBUTING.md AGENTS.md CODE-CONTRACTS.md DEVELOPMENT.md
bugs.observed: Zero in all five. MAINTAINER.md section 4, the per-change checklist, has eight steps covering consumers, fixtures, diagrams, docs, manifest/map/skill_files registration, which tests to run, and the commit shape — and no step touching either register.
bugs.expected: The checklist names the registers: an entry closed when its defect is fixed, an entry added when one is found and not fixed in the same breath, and the version stamp refreshed.
bugs.mechanism: The registers arrived late and were documented only in their own skills. Every other obligation in the checklist has a gate that fails without it, so the checklist is a convenience for those; for the registers it is the only instruction there is, and it is silent. Nothing fails when BUGS.json is stale.
bugs.fix: MAINTAINER.md section 4 gains step 8 (update the registers) and renumbers the commit step to 9, which now also says the message names the entries it closes. The artifact map gains a row for both registers. CONTRIBUTING.md gains a bullet in the pre-PR list, and AGENTS.md says to read the relevant register before starting and update it when finished.
bugs.verification: grep for BUGS.json across the five maintainer-facing docs went from 0 hits to 4. No gate is possible -- no test can tell that a commit resolved a defect -- and each of the four places says so, so the absence of enforcement is documented rather than implied. The doc gates (duplication ratchet, mermaid accuracy, comment format, persona drift) and blast-radius still pass.
bugs.found_by: reviewing commit 9f41091 (codex, "planning: resolve bug report items"): 40 files and 789 insertions, zero changes to BUGS.json or TODO.json
bugs.notes: Written immediately after the review that found it, and the same review is the evidence: commit 9f41091 met every gated obligation and missed this one. The temptation while fixing it was to defer closing this very entry because a subagent holds BUGS.json in another worktree -- which is the same excuse the step exists to remove, so it was closed here and the conflict left to be resolved.

bugs.title: add-ui-story-links.sh could not reject an unknown work unit on bash 3.2, because its guard ran in a pipeline subshell
bugs.reproduce: nix develop --command bash32-run planning/tests/test-plan-commands.sh  # from commit 9f41091
bugs.observed: add-ui-story-links accepted an unknown related work unit. Passed under bash 5.3, failed on 3.2 only.
bugs.expected: W99 is not in the inventory, so the call refuses with exit 66.
bugs.mechanism: The validating loop was the last stage of a pipeline, so it ran in a subshell and plan_die exited that subshell rather than the script. On bash 5 set -e then aborts on the pipeline status; on bash 3.2 it does not. Isolated: `set -euo pipefail; printf a | while read x; do exit 66; done; echo CONTINUED` prints CONTINUED on 3.2 and aborts on 5.3.
bugs.fix: Split on commas with IFS and a for loop, so the guard runs in the current shell. No other guard in the repo has this shape — checked.
bugs.verification: test-plan-commands passes on both shells; before the fix it passed on 5.3 and failed on 3.2. Catalogued as the pipeline-subshell-guard rule, documentation-only because the shape spans several lines and a pipeline-while is fine when it is not guarding.
bugs.found_by: reviewing commit 9f41091 (codex) — the bash 3.2 leg of ./verify-both-shells.sh
bugs.notes: The floor earning its keep: a guard that reads correctly and does nothing is worse than no guard, and only 3.2 showed it. Codex met every gated obligation in that commit and this one had no gate.

bugs.title: Every test install wrote its throwaway --target into the real XDG config of the user, 1894 lines of it
bugs.observed: 1895 lines, 120K: 1894 of them /tmp paths from test runs, one real entry.
bugs.expected: A one-off --target is not a location the user chose to remember.
bugs.mechanism: select_targets called save_custom_location on the non-interactive --target path, so every test that installed into a temp directory appended to a persistent user config file.
bugs.fix: 9f41091 (codex) removed the call. The interactive path still saves, which is where a user does choose a location.
bugs.verification: No new entries after a --target install; the interactive caller at 40-selection.sh:129 is untouched, so the feature survives.
bugs.found_by: reviewing 9f41091 - the diff removed a call, and the file it wrote to turned out to hold 120K of test debris
bugs.notes: The stale entries are gone: pruned 2026-08-21 from 1895 lines to the single live one, with a backup at custom-locations.bak. Measured before pruning: only 1 of the 1895 directories still existed, so load_custom_locations already filtered the rest with [ -d ] and the menu was never visibly wrong. The objection was the write itself, plus the fact that a leaked test root that did still exist would have been offered as an install target.

bugs.title: The per-test TMPDIR leaked for 67 of the tests, because a test setting its own EXIT trap replaces the one lib-test.sh installs
bugs.reproduce: source planning/tests/lib-test.sh; trap 'rm -rf x' EXIT; exit 0   # then look for /tmp/t.?????
bugs.observed: The root survives. 67 test files set their own EXIT trap, and six stale roots were sitting in /tmp.
bugs.expected: Each test root is removed when the test ends.
bugs.mechanism: lib-test.sh installs an EXIT trap at source time; bash keeps one EXIT trap per shell, so a test that traps EXIT afterwards silently discards it. Commit 1044857 introduced this, and the assertion written with it only covered a shell that sets no trap of its own.
bugs.fix: 9f41091 (codex): run-tests.sh exports AI_SKILLS_TEST_RUN_ID, lib-test.sh writes it into each root as .ai-skills-test-run-id, and the runner sweeps only roots carrying this run id.
bugs.verification: A run leaves no /tmp/t.????? behind. The marker keeps the sweep safe under concurrency, which was the objection behind refusing to sweep at all.
bugs.found_by: reviewing 9f41091 - its comment named the trap hazard, and the reproduction confirmed it
bugs.notes: Better than the decision recorded in T10: a run was said to be unable to distinguish its own leftovers from a concurrent run live directories. A run id distinguishes them.

bugs.title: On stock macOS the registry fallback runs a real benchmark agent with no time bound at all
bugs.reproduce: On a host with neither setsid nor timeout/gtimeout: start-worker.sh calls launch_agent isolated "${WORKER_TIMEOUT:-45m}" - mode becomes registry, no timeout binary is found, and lib-agent.sh warns and launches anyway.
bugs.observed: lib-agent.sh:140-148 prints "registry fallback cannot bound the agent to 45m" and then runs the agent unbounded, because cmd gets no timeout prefix.
bugs.expected: A worker that cannot be bounded is refused, as it was before: the setsid path still returns 69 in the same situation.
bugs.mechanism: 9f41091 added an isolated mode that degrades setsid to a registry fallback when setsid is missing, which is stock macOS. The same change turned the missing-timeout refusal into a warning for that fallback only. The two degradations compose: no process group and no clock.
bugs.fix: lib-agent.sh grew a third rung below timeout/gtimeout: in registry mode only, launch_agent parses the spec (<n>s/<n>m/<n>h, 64 on anything else) and starts _agent_watchdog as a background sibling of the agent. The watchdog polls kill -0 in one-second steps, then TERMs the ps-walked tree and escalates to KILL after 5s; wait_agent calls _agent_watchdog_stop, which kills the watchdog and its in-flight sleep. The setsid path still returns 69, and a present timeout/gtimeout still wins, so the watchdog is never used when a real bound exists.
bugs.verification: test-safeguards.sh launches fake agents with a PATH holding neither timeout nor gtimeout: a 2s-bounded sleeper and its descendant are both killed, a TERM-ignoring agent is KILLed, an agent that exits on its own is not killed and leaves no watchdog or sleep, 45x is refused with 64, a stubbed timeout binary is used with no watchdog started, and the setsid path still returns 69. Mutations that each fail exactly one of those: never starting the watchdog (the B13 regression), TERMing the pid instead of the tree, dropping _agent_watchdog_stop, TERMing the watchdog without its sleep child, one long sleep instead of the poll, accepting any spec, skipping the timeout binary, starting the watchdog even when timeout is present, and turning the setsid 69 back into a warning.
bugs.found_by: reviewing 9f41091 after being asked about the setsid fix specifically
bugs.notes: These callers launch real worker and reviewer agents that spend real tokens, so an unbounded run is the expensive failure, not an inconvenient one. The new tests in test-safeguards.sh cover the registry wiring and prove the nohup/setsid/open shims refuse, but assert nothing about the timeout path. Options: keep the refusal in registry mode too; or implement a shell watchdog (background sleep plus kill of the registered pid and its ps-walked descendants) so the bound survives without GNU coreutils. The second is more work and is the only one that makes a macOS benchmark run at all.

bugs.title: The documented renders sort ids as strings, so item 10 lands between item 1 and item 2
bugs.reproduce: jq -r 'def prank: {urgent:0,high:1,normal:2,low:3,someday:4}[.priority]//5; def srank: {blocking:0,major:1,minor:2,cosmetic:3}[.severity]//4; [.bugs[]] | sort_by(prank, srank, .id)[] | .id' BUGS.json
bugs.observed: B2 B10 B13 B3 B4 B5 B7 B8 B9 B11 B12 B6 B1 - B10 sits between B2 and B3. The todo queue renders T13 T14 T15 before T21, and T5 T6 after T31.
bugs.expected: Numeric order within a priority band: B2 B3 B4 B5 B6 B7 ... B13.
bugs.mechanism: Seven snippets across the two SKILL.md files sort with sort_by(rank, .id) or sort_by(prank, srank, .id), where .id is a string, so jq compares byte-wise and "B10" < "B3". jq has no natural-sort builtin.
bugs.fix: def idkey: [(. | scan("[0-9]+") | tonumber)?, .]; added beside the existing rank defs in all seven snippets across both SKILL.md files, and every sort_by now passes (.id | idkey). Ids stay free-form, so nothing had to be renumbered and the commit messages that reference T30 and B8 still resolve. The id row in both field tables says why the def is there, so it does not get removed as noise.
bugs.verification: The documented snippets were extracted from SKILL.md and run verbatim against the real registers: top-level normal tasks read T1 T2 T3 T4 T5 T6 T13 T14 T15 T16 T17 T21 T23 T24 T26 T27 T30 T31, and a sub-task renders under its parent. Mutation: dropping idkey from one snippet gives T1 T13 T14 T15 T16 T17 T2 T21 ... T3 T30 T31 T4 T5 T6. A first mutation probe looked green because within the high band the ids happen to sort identically either way -- the normal band is where it shows.
bugs.found_by: a bug report written against 1.4.2 by an earlier session (bug-report-old-version.md), re-verified against the current registers
bugs.notes: Live, and it produced misleading output all through this session without being noticed - every register render printed above is in the wrong order. Two candidate fixes. Zero-padded ids make lexical sort correct with no snippet change, but require renumbering ids that commit messages already reference (T30, B8), because a mix of T5 and T05 sorts wrong anyway. A derived key - def idkey: [(. | scan("[0-9]+") | tonumber)?, .] - keeps ids free-form and is the only option that also respects the skills own T1 -> T1a convention, placing a child immediately after its parent in a flat render; length-then-lexical looked cheaper but drifts T1a to the end. Its stated cost, a def copied into seven snippets, is already the pattern in these files: the rank and prank/srank defs are duplicated across all of them today, so this adds no new kind of debt.

bugs.title: A benchmark test calls timeout, which macOS does not have
bugs.observed: timeout: command not found, after every earlier assertion in the file had passed.
bugs.expected: Either a portable timeout, or the test degrading honestly on a platform without one.
bugs.mechanism: GNU coreutils timeout is not on macOS. PORTABILITY.md already lists it under gnu-only-tools with a gtimeout fallback; this call site predates the rule or was missed because the gate does not scan benchmark tests the same way.
bugs.fix: Both `timeout 60s` wrappers removed rather than given a gtimeout fallback. What they wrapped is a shell script in the fixture that writes a file and exits, so the cap could only fire on a defect and would then report a timeout instead of the defect.
bugs.verification: The test passes and takes 5 seconds against a 60s cap per call. It was the only test in an 80-test suite with a wall clock, and the only reason this file could not run on macOS.
bugs.notes: Asked directly: why a timeout at all. lib-agent.sh does bound a real agent and handles timeout/gtimeout properly with an explicit refusal — that one is a genuine need, these two were a hedge. A `sleep 1` remains in the codex-worker fake, with a stated reason: the runner must capture a live process group. That is a real synchronisation point and wants a handshake rather than a sleep; recorded as T29.

bugs.title: create-plan.sh creates the plans root before validating the plan name, so a refused call leaves a directory behind
bugs.observed: Refuses with "Plan directory name must be kebab-case", and /tmp/mkdir-probe exists afterwards.
bugs.expected: Nothing on disk changes when the call is refused.
bugs.mechanism: The mkdir -p added in 9f41091 sits in the argument case around line 53; the kebab-case check and the refuse-existing check are at 63 and 65. CODE-CONTRACTS.md contract 2 puts anything irreversible last.
bugs.fix: The mkdir moved out of the argument case to just after the guards -- the kebab-case check, the refuse-existing check and plan_require_safe_value -- and is now conditional on the directory being absent. An explicit path still creates the directory that holds it; a call about to be refused no longer does.
bugs.verification: test-create-plan-explicit-root.sh gains two assertions: a non-kebab name is refused with 64 and its parent does not exist afterwards, and an occupied plan directory is refused with 73. Mutation: moving the mkdir back into the argument case fails the first with "a refused call created its parent directory". test-coverage-gaps and test-plan-commands still pass, which is what exercises the bare-name path that does not create anything itself.
bugs.notes: The mkdir itself is right - an explicit path should be able to create its parent. Only the order is wrong: move it after both guards.

bugs.title: The planning-bugs.json plan artifact was added with no writer and no diagram update
bugs.observed: Readers everywhere - plan_document_path, plan_document_kind, plan-context-lib, the plan-content usage text, test-document-id-parity - and nothing that creates the file. Only the test writes one.
bugs.expected: Either a script that produces it, or a stated reason it is written by an agent by hand.
bugs.mechanism: The id was wired through every reader consistently, which is the hard part; the producer and the documentation were not. MAINTAINER.md section 4 step 4 requires the ARCHITECTURE.md diagram to be updated in the same change when a plan artifact is added, and that file is untouched.
bugs.fix: add-planning-bug.sh writes the register, in the shape add-fix-claim.sh established when fixes.md needed the same thing: validate everything before touching the file, snapshot the plan, append through plan_atomic_write. The file follows the bug-report skill schema, so that skill jq recipes read a plan register unchanged. Registered in PACKAGE-MANIFEST.txt, PACKAGE-MAP.tsv and the prod arm of skill_files, and both the artifact and its writer are now in the section 5 diagram, which MAINTAINER.md step 4 requires.
bugs.verification: test-add-planning-bug.sh: the register does not exist until written and asking for it gives 66; first use creates it and the entry is read back rather than trusted from an exit code; a backslash and embedded quotes survive; six refusals each with their own code (73 duplicate, 64 bad id, 64 missing reproduction, 64 unknown severity, 64 status fixed, 66 missing plan, 65 damaged register) and the damaged file is left untouched; and the bug-report skill own render lists both entries. Mutations caught: dropping the duplicate check, widening the status enum, appending to a damaged register. All 10 mermaid diagrams render with the new nodes under mmdc. The read-back guard is tested rather than merely asserted to be untestable: a jq on PATH passes every call through except the append, the one carrying --arg now, which it answers with nothing. That call then refuses with 70, prints no success line, and leaves the zero-byte register in place for inspection, with a control on a clean plan proving the seam is what makes the difference. Removing the guard now fails two assertions.
bugs.notes: The intent was inferred, not known: the test seeds {"bugs":[]}, the id is grouped with the optional artifacts, a missing file is asserted to give 66, and planning/SKILL.md never mentions it. So it reads as a plan-scoped defect register in the bug-report skill format. Writing the writer rather than documenting hand-authoring follows this repo own precedent, commit 3783dab. Building it turned up that jq handed an empty input never runs its filter, so the first version wrote a zero-byte register and reported success; the guard against that is now covered by a PATH seam rather than left as a known gap, because MAINTAINER.md step 3 asks for a test of the actionable-error path and a backstop with no test is a claim, not a guard.

bugs.title: A second --skill silently discards the first, so the installer installs something other than what was asked
bugs.observed: Selected skills: bug-report — and only bug-report is installed. Reversing the two flags installs only todo. No warning either way.
bugs.expected: Both skills installed, or a refusal naming the conflict. Discarding an argument the caller supplied is the one thing it must not do silently.
bugs.mechanism: installer/src/10-cli-args.sh:60 assigns SKILL_SELECTION="$2" as a scalar, so each --skill overwrites the previous. --all takes the array path; --skill never did.
bugs.verification: README.md:133-135 documents it: "--skill takes one selection... Repeating the flag does not accumulate; the last one wins", and --skill todo,bug-report installs both. Verified: Selected skills: todo bug-report, both directories written. The behaviour matches its documentation, so it is not a defect.
bugs.found_by: installing the two register skills for the user in one command
bugs.notes: Recorded from the install itself without reading the flag documentation first. The residual objection -- that silently discarding a supplied argument is worse than refusing it -- is a design preference, not a defect, and belongs in TODO.json.
